## Warning — Uncalibrated Model, Report Still Evolving
This is the **Phase 4** version of the report. Network geometry has been
corrected from OSM using imagery evidence (deck lane count, merge-junction
type, pier/bay structure), but baseline demand is still **hypothetical**
(engineering judgment, not a field count). Per the project's Hard Rule 5,
every number in this report is a **mean ± 95% confidence interval over 10
independent seeds**. **All six planned scenarios (S0 through S5) have now
been built and simulated** — S0 (do-nothing), S1 (signalized, two control
modes), S2 (left-turn removal + a physical median U-turn, three sensitivity
distances), S3 (asymmetric roundabout, two variants), S4 (channelization),
and S5 (hybrid/creative, three variants: metering plus two bypass priority
designs) — plus a new **combined scenario (S2+S4)** — **13 control
variants, 650 official SUMO runs** (5 lambda x 10 seeds each). A **separate
diagnostic experiment** (100 more runs, outside the formal registry) also
reran S0/S1 with SUMO's default (non-aggressive) behavioral parameters
instead of this study's tuned-aggressive set, to separate "the signal's own
effect" from "the effect of uncalibrated aggressive behavior" (Section 6).
**This version is therefore the first complete (not necessarily final)
Phase-4 ranking** — still conditional on real calibration (Section 10),
not the project's final conclusion. Every number here is valid only for
**relative scenario comparison**, not as a prediction of real-world
absolute values. **S5's detailed qualitative/SWOT analysis and two rounds
of geometric/control revision on its bypass were completed** (Sections 7
and 8): both revisions were honestly **rejected** — neither produced a
reliable improvement (Section 7, mechanism 5). By contrast, **a new
combined scenario (S2+S4) was built and simulated**, giving this study's
best safety result (an 80-84% collision reduction versus S0 at lambda >=
1.0, significant) — now at the top of the preliminary ranking (Section 9).
What remains is a more careful geometric design for S3 and genuine active
control (not a priority/geometry adjustment) for the S5 bypass — see
Section 12.
:::

## 1. Executive Summary

The Seyedi under-bridge intersection in Kerman is where Imam Reza Highway
(on the bridge deck, east-west axis) crosses Seyedi Blvd / Shahid Soleimani
Blvd (under the bridge, north-south axis). Through movement on the bridge
deck is not a problem; the real bottleneck is the **turning movements under
the bridge**, which — absent channelization or a signal — are effectively
handled as an informal, semi-formal traffic circle (weaving).

This study built a fully reproducible pipeline with SUMO micro-simulation
that regenerates everything, from satellite imagery and OSM to the final
report, with one command (`make all`). As of this version:

- **The existing condition (S0)**, as the comparison baseline, was
  simulated at 5 demand levels (lambda from 0.6 to 1.4 times the assumed
  baseline demand) x 10 independent seeds (50 runs).
- **S1 (signal)** in two modes (fixed-time / actuated), **S2 (left-turn
  removal + physical median U-turn)** at three sensitivity distances
  (150/250/350 m), **S3 (asymmetric roundabout)** in two options
  (constrained / open center span), and **S4 (channelization)** — each on
  the same 5-lambda x 10-seed grid. **1,100 SUMO runs** in total across 11
  control variants.
- **A separate diagnostic experiment** (100 more runs): S0 and S1-fixed
  rerun with SUMO's **default** behavioral parameters (not this study's
  aggressive tuning) to separate "the signal's own effect" from "the effect
  of uncalibrated aggressive behavior."
- **Key, unexpected S1 finding:** in this uncalibrated model, converting to
  a signal (either mode) not only failed to **reduce** mean delay, it
  **increased** it by up to 105% (at high demand), and raised collisions by
  up to 12x. **The behavioral diagnostic (Section 6)** sharpened this: even
  with SUMO's default behavior, S1 is still 36-57% more delayed than S0 (so
  most of the delay effect really does come from the signal design under
  under-saturated demand), but collisions with default behavior nearly
  vanished — i.e., **the collision explosion is almost entirely a product
  of signal-induced queuing interacting with uncalibrated aggressive
  behavior, not the signal itself.**
- **S4 performed essentially identically to S0** (no statistically
  significant difference at any lambda, neither better nor worse) —
  channelization alone made no measurable difference.
- **S2 (full version, with a real U-turn)** is somewhat more conservative
  than its first, simplified cut — now slightly **worse** than S0 at
  low/mid lambda (7-12%, significant), but at lambda=1.4 (peak demand) it
  remains **not significantly different** from S0 and is directionally
  safer. Sensitivity to the U-turn distance (150/250/350 m) was negligible.
- **S3 (roundabout) is significantly worse than S0 at low/mid demand**
  (12-20% more delay) — the classic roundabout pattern (a fixed geometric
  cost at low demand). **A geometric revision in this session** (an arc
  shape instead of a straight line, and reverting the ring from two lanes
  back to one after an experiment showed two lanes *increases* collisions)
  eliminated teleports entirely and visibly reduced collisions — see
  `scenarios/S3_roundabout/README.md`.
- **S5 (hybrid) was built, simulated, and — across this and a follow-up
  session — put through two rounds of geometric/control revision on its
  bypass variant** (both options: roundabout + metering, roundabout +
  priority north-south bypass). The two variants diverge sharply:
  **metering** genuinely improves on the bare S3-constrained ring at peak
  demand (max queue 106 m vs. the bare ring's 147 m) and is also more
  robust (its worst single seed at lambda=1.4 is only 44 s / 483
  collisions); its 20 s cycle was empirically checked, not just assumed.
  **The north-south bypass** went through two rounds of revision and failed
  honestly both times. Round 1: its documented geometric conflict (a
  netconvert "intersecting left turns" warning) was fully resolved exactly
  as netconvert's own diagnostic suggested (widening the junction radius) —
  but this fix did not produce a reliable improvement: at lambda=1.4, mean
  delay actually rose to 61.7 s (+126% vs. S0), no longer statistically
  significant (p=0.13) because variance exploded — 9 of 10 seeds cluster
  around a more reasonable ~42 s, but 1 of 10 seeds collapses completely
  (242 s delay, 6,009 collisions in a single run). Round 2, testing the
  resulting hypothesis directly: the bypass's unconditional priority
  (edge priority 80, `pass="true"`) was lowered to a normal yielding
  priority (30, below the ring's 50, no `pass`) — but the result was worse,
  not better: at lambda=1.4, collisions rose to 1,526.5 per run, this time
  **uniformly across all 10 seeds** (428-4,498 collisions each) rather than
  a rare collapse, and the delay/collision differences from S0 became
  cleanly significant at every lambda level (p<0.05). Neither priority
  scheme works; the conflict point itself, not its priority design, is the
  problem — see Section 12 for what a real fix likely requires.
- **A new combined scenario, S2+S4, was built and simulated** (per
  next-step item 3, Section 12): two independent, low-risk fixes — S2
  (left-turn removal + U-turn) and S4 (right-turn channelization) — were
  combined on one network with no new code, since their affected junctions
  are entirely separate. The result is **this study's best safety finding**:
  an 80-84% reduction in collisions versus S0 at lambda >= 1.0 (all
  significant, large effect sizes), a max queue length down to 71% lower,
  and delay at lambda=1.4 even directionally better than S0 — with no
  active control at all.
- **Preliminary summary (not final, based on complete data for all 6 main
  scenarios, both S5-bypass revision attempts, and the S2+S4 combination):**
  **S2+S4 combined is now at the top of the current ranking**; **S4 and S0
  alone effectively tied, second tier**; **S2 alone close behind, with a
  real edge at peak demand**; **S3 and S5's metering variant need more
  careful geometric/control design before a final judgment, but show a
  genuinely promising signal**; **S1 and both of S5's tested bypass designs
  are not recommended as-is**. See Section 9 (ranking) and Section 8
  (SWOT) for detail.

## 2. Problem Statement and Background

### 2.1 Location and nature of the problem

The Seyedi under-bridge intersection consists of two entirely separate
levels:

- **The bridge deck (upper level):** Imam Reza Highway, east-west axis,
  high design speed, unproblematic through flow.
- **Under the bridge (lower, at-grade level):** Seyedi Blvd from the north
  and Shahid Soleimani Blvd from the south, together with four loop ramps
  that move traffic between the two levels.

The core problem is the space under the bridge: no signal, no defined
channelization, and no formal right-of-way for left turns. The result
behaves like an informal traffic circle (informal weaving), where drivers
negotiate right-of-way moment to moment rather than by a predefined rule.

### 2.2 What the satellite imagery taught us

A systematic review of Google Earth imagery (Phase 0; see
`docs/imagery_review.md`), and in particular a close inspection of the 2012
image (when the bridge structure was still bare and the piers fully
visible), revealed a determining physical fact not obvious from today's
maps at first glance:

> Under the bridge, along the east-west axis, the space is divided into
> **7 bays** (3 west + 1 center + 3 east). Of the three bays on each side,
> only the one **adjacent to the center** is open to traffic; the two outer
> bays on each side are completely closed and are part of the bridge's
> structural body — not usable open space. The center bay is also
> currently kept deliberately closed.

This finding corrected the Phase-0 first impression ("one continuous open
plaza"): what actually exists under the bridge is **two discrete choke
points** (the west open bay and the east open bay) with a closed structural
wall between them, not one continuous open space. This physical fact places
a hard ceiling on any future geometric design in this study (including the
feasibility of a modern roundabout in S3), and is recorded in
`config/assumptions.yml` under `bridge_geometry.span_structure`.

### 2.3 Why microsimulation, and why SUMO?

Classical capacity analysis (HCM) was built for standard four-leg
intersections / roundabouts, and its assumptions (orderly queuing,
discrete, classifiable movements) are exactly what is violated at this
site: informal weaving behavior, a high motorcycle share with inter-lane
filtering, and two discrete choke points separated by an unconventional
structural element. A microsimulation that models each vehicle
individually (not just aggregate flow) is the only method that can capture
this complexity. SUMO (Simulation of Urban MObility) was chosen because it
is open-source and scriptable, so the entire pipeline (network, demand,
behavior, execution, analysis) can be built programmatically and
reproducibly — a prerequisite for the project's Hard Rule 1.

## 3. Modeling Methodology: SUMO in Plain Language

This section explains the technical workflow without assuming prior SUMO
knowledge.

### 3.1 Network — "the street map for the simulation engine"

SUMO needs a network file (`.net.xml`) containing nodes (junctions), edges
(street segments), lanes, and the right-of-way/signal logic at each
junction. This network was built from OpenStreetMap data with `netconvert`:

1. A bounding box at least 400 m from the intersection center in every
   direction was pulled from OSM.
2. `netconvert` converted this raw data into a simulatable network — with
   flags to preserve layer elevation (`--osm.layer-elevation`, so the
   bridge deck and the at-grade layer below it are not accidentally
   merged), ramp guessing, and merging very close junctions.
3. **Mandatory visual check:** deck/underpass level separation was drawn
   and confirmed by elevation-based coloring (@fig-layer-check) — per
   `CLAUDE.md`'s explicit emphasis, the single most likely failure point of
   this model.
4. For greater fidelity (Phase 2), imagery-evidence corrections (deck lane
   count, merge-junction behavior type) were applied **directly to the
   intermediate plain-XML text files** with a Python script and the network
   rebuilt — not by hand-editing in the `netedit` GUI tool — so every
   change is Git-trackable and reproducible (Hard Rule 2).

![Visual grade-separation check: red = bridge deck (z>0), blue = at-grade network (z=0).](../outputs/figures/network_layer_check_zoom.png){#fig-layer-check width=85%}

### 3.2 Demand — "how many vehicles, from where to where"

Unlike regional studies that need a full origin-destination (OD) matrix, for
a single intersection, **entry volume per approach + turning ratios** is
far less data-hungry and far more attainable. The `jtrrouter` tool does
exactly this: given each approach's volume and its through/right/left split
at each fork, it builds individual vehicle routes. Baseline demand (see
`config/assumptions.yml`), absent a field count, comes from engineering
judgment (lane count x approximate lane capacity), and is therefore treated
as a sensitivity factor (lambda) rather than a fixed number.

### 3.3 Fleet and driver behavior — "not everyone drives the same"

Six vehicle classes (passenger car, motorcycle at a 30% share, taxi, pickup,
bus, light truck) each have their own behavioral parameters
(`config/vtypes.yml`). Key points:

- **High motorcycle share (30%):** reflects a qualitative reading of the
  imagery (not a count) — the top priority for future calibration.
- **Sublane model enabled** (`--lateral-resolution 0.8`): without it, SUMO
  treats each lane as a rigid unit and motorcycle filtering between lanes
  (real, imagery-observed behavior) cannot be represented.
- **More aggressive parameters than SUMO defaults:** shorter follower time
  gap (`tau`), higher right-of-way disregard (`jmIgnoreFoeProb`), and
  higher lane-change assertiveness (`lcAssertive`) — especially for
  motorcycles — to reflect close-following Iranian driving culture. Every
  one of these parameters is flagged `sensitivity: true`; as Section 10
  will show, these same parameters are likely the **primary cause** of
  S1's counter-intuitive finding.

### 3.4 Experiment design — multi-scenario x multi-demand x multi-seed

No stochastic simulation result should be judged from a single run —
randomness in driver behavior (`sigma`) and route assignment alone can
shift the outcome. Per the project's Hard Rule 5, every combination
(scenario x demand level) is therefore repeated **10 times with independent
seeds** (1 through 10), and the mean ± 95% confidence interval (t
distribution, appropriate for a small sample) is reported. Demand level is
also tested at 5 scale factors (lambda = 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4 times the
assumed baseline demand) to determine over what demand range the scenario
ranking stays stable.

### 3.5 KPIs and the statistical comparison method

Every run produces: `tripinfo` (trip duration, time loss, waiting, per
vehicle), `summary` (did all demand actually enter the network?),
`statistic` (total collision count), `queue` (per-lane queue length over
time — for checking ramp-overflow risk), and the `SSM` device (surrogate
safety measures TTC/DRAC/PET). Because every seed generates the same
baseline demand across all scenarios (shared seeds), scenarios are compared
with a **paired t-test** and **paired Cohen's d** — not just a percentage
difference in means, which can be misleading.

## 4. Scenarios — Detailed Description

The table below shows each scenario's current status; a full description of
each follows, and each has its own design folder with a `README.md`
(`scenarios/<code>/README.md`).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scenario-status
#| tbl-cap: "Build status of each scenario"
import yaml
from IPython.display import Markdown
import pandas as pd
scen_cfg = yaml.safe_load(open("../config/scenarios.yml", encoding="utf-8"))["scenarios"]
status_en = {"built": "Built and simulated", "planned": "Conceptual design (not yet built)"}
rows = [{"Code": k, "Title": v["label_en"], "Status": status_en[v["status"]]} for k, v in scen_cfg.items()]
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False))
```

### S0 — Do-Nothing (existing condition)

The comparison baseline for every other scenario. Geometry is exactly what
exists today: no signal, no formal channelization. Merge points under the
bridge are modeled with a `zipper` junction model — SUMO's special
representation of safe "first-come-first-served" fade-in merging, exactly
the behavior observed in the imagery and confirmed by the user at
Checkpoint 1 ("left turns are currently free and informal").

### S1 — Signalized Intersection

**Topological finding before design:** network inspection showed that
under the bridge there is **no real single junction node** (simultaneously
having in-degree >= 2 and out-degree >= 2) — OSM decomposed it into a chain
of about 24 small ramp/merge/diverge nodes, exactly consistent with Phase
0's "quasi-roundabout with no channelization" description. This was
discussed with the user, and the following decision was made (see
`config/assumptions.yml -> signal_design_S1` for the full rationale):

> Rather than the high-risk option of merging these ~24 nodes into one
> artificial junction, or one shared (joined) signal program across a
> ~150 m chain of merge points that do not actually happen simultaneously
> in reality, **every real merge node (in-degree >= 2) inside the weaving
> zone gets its own independent traffic light** — with a shared cycle
> length computed by the classic **Webster** method.

The optimal cycle length for design demand (lambda=1.0) was computed:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-webster
#| tbl-cap: "Webster cycle calculation for S1 (per src/08_webster_timing.py)"
timing = yaml.safe_load(open("../config/signal_timing_S1.yml", encoding="utf-8"))
rows = [
    {"Parameter": "Critical flow ratio, phase A (N-S through)", "Value": f"{timing['critical_flow_ratios']['y_A']:.3f}"},
    {"Parameter": "Critical flow ratio, phase B (deck turns)", "Value": f"{timing['critical_flow_ratios']['y_B']:.3f}"},
    {"Parameter": "Y (sum of critical ratios)", "Value": f"{timing['critical_flow_ratios']['Y']:.3f}"},
    {"Parameter": "Webster optimal cycle length (s)", "Value": f"{timing['cycle_length_s']['final_used_s']:.1f}"},
    {"Parameter": "Effective green, phase A / phase B (s)", "Value": f"{timing['green_split_s']['phase_A_ns_through']:.1f} / {timing['green_split_s']['phase_B_bridge_turns']:.1f}"},
]
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False))
```

With Y ~ 0.59 (clearly under-saturated at design demand), the optimal cycle
came out to about 42 seconds. This cycle is applied unchanged across all 5
lambda levels in the **fixed-time** variant; the **actuated** variant
instead uses SUMO's default gap-out logic, which shortens/extends green
based on actual vehicle presence.

**An interesting side finding during network construction:** of 10
candidate nodes (in-degree >= 2 within the weaving radius), only **5**
actually had conflicting movements (foes) and received a meaningful
multi-phase program; the other 5 were conflict-free merges and
`netconvert` itself set them to "permanently green" — showing that part of
what looked at first glance like a "conflict point" was actually just a
free, non-conflicting connection.

### S2 — Turn Restriction + Physical U-Turn (RCUT / Median U-Turn)

**Status: built and simulated (version 2 — full).** International
equivalent: RCUT (Restricted Crossing U-Turn) or Median U-Turn (the
Michigan left) — the direct left turn under the bridge is removed, and a
vehicle instead continues through/right and completes its move at a U-turn
away from the intersection (per the user's explicit constraint: away from
the bridge's center, since deck speed is high).

Inspecting the diverge nodes inside the weaving zone identified 9 real
decision points, each choosing between through and one of
left-turn/right-turn; of these 9, **5** had a left-turn option, and that
connection was removed from the plain-XML. The two long deck edges
(eastbound/westbound) were each split at two points (+-D meters from the
weave center) via **genuine arc-length interpolation on the edge's real
curved shape**, with a short U-turn connector added at each split point. D
was built at three sensitivity levels: **150 / 250 / 350 meters**. Demand
is routed with a new `extra_turn_rules` mechanism: 15% of through-traffic
at each split point (matching the removed left-turn share) actually travels
the "through -> U-turn -> return -> right turn" path — not just a
statistical reassignment of destination. See
`scenarios/S2_rcut/README.md`.

### S3 — Asymmetric Roundabout (two options)

**Status: built and simulated (both options).** Per the user's Checkpoint
decision (2026-09-14: "build both, comparatively"), both options were
built. Since there is no single real junction node under the bridge (same
finding as S1), rather than merging/removing the existing ~24-node chain, a
**4-edge counter-clockwise ring** was added between the four real junction
nodes closest to the two open bays (the nodes nearest the north/south
approaches and the west/east open spans) — **without removing** any
existing topology. Ring connections get a high numeric priority and
`pass="true"` (unconditional right-of-way for circulating traffic):

- **`constrained`:** the ring alone, limited to the two existing open bays.
- **`full`:** the same ring plus a direct east-west chord, standing in for
  the (structurally conditional) opened center bay — subject to a
  structural engineer's sign-off, outside this traffic study's scope.

Both variants completed validation runs (all vehicles finished); the
`constrained` variant showed a small (0.1%) "wrong-lane" teleport rate,
most likely from a lane-count mismatch between the ring's single-lane edges
and the multi-lane real edges — see `scenarios/S3_roundabout/README.md`
for this implementation's explicit limitations (the ring geometry is a
straight-line-between-4-points approximation, not an engineered
deflection/island design).

### S4 — Channelization + Free Right Turn

**Status: built and simulated.** The least aggressive geometric
intervention among the scenarios: the same 5 real-conflict merge nodes from
S1 were reverted from `zipper` to `priority`, and each node's main through
connection got `pass="true"` (unconditional priority, matching normal
traffic-engineering convention that the mainline does not yield for a
channelized right-turn merge); the channelized right turn kept normal
minor/yield priority. No new topology node was needed. "Removing curbside
parking" was never modeled in the baseline, so it has no network effect
here — see `scenarios/S4_channelization/README.md`.

### S5 — Hybrid / Creative

**Status: built, simulated, and geometrically/control-wise revised (the
first two of three candidate ideas; the bypass tested under two different
priority designs).** All three built variants sit on the S3-constrained
ring infrastructure: **metering** (roundabout + a single-node metering
signal on the west leg, a 20 s cycle empirically checked against
alternatives), **oneway_priority** (roundabout + a direct two-way
north-south bypass with unconditional priority even higher than the ring
itself), and **oneway_yield** (the same bypass with normal yielding
priority instead — lower than the ring, no unconditional right-of-way).
Unlike S3-full's chord, the bypass does not need the center bay opened,
since Seyedi Blvd already crosses at grade. The third idea (opening the
center bay for light-vehicle movements) conceptually overlaps with S3-full
and was not built. All three built variants perform worse than S0, but at
very different severity: metering improves on the bare S3-constrained ring
at peak demand; the bypass, under **both** priority designs tested (even
after its documented geometric conflict was fixed), remains either fragile
or uniformly weak at peak demand — not because of resistance to fixing, but
because the conflict point itself is the problem, not its priority design
(see Section 7 for the full analysis). See `scenarios/S5_hybrid/README.md`.

### S2+S4 combined — left-turn removal + U-turn, simultaneous with right-turn channelization

**Status: built and simulated (this session, per next-step item 3 in
Section 12).** This scenario goes beyond the six main S0-S5 options — a
direct response to this study's recurring finding that "removing a
geometric conflict without adding active control" (S2, S4) performs at
least as well as, and sometimes better than, adding uncalibrated active
control (S1, S5). The question: can these two low-risk fixes be applied to
the same network at once? **No new logic was written** —
`scenarios/S2_S4_combined/build_network.py` calls the two existing S2
(`apply_s2_modifications`, D=250 m baseline) and S4
(`retype_nodes_to_priority` + `mark_free_right_connections`) functions, in
sequence, on one shared plain-XML. The combination is possible without
interference because S2's nodes (diverges) and S4's nodes (merges) are two
entirely separate sets of physical junctions — see
`scenarios/S2_S4_combined/README.md` for the full node table and
confirmation of no overlap.

## 5. Results: All 6 Main Scenarios Plus One Combination

```{python}
#| echo: false
SCEN_LABELS = [("s0", "S0"), ("s1_fixed", "S1-fixed"), ("s1_actuated", "S1-actuated"),
               ("s2", "S2 (D=250m)"), ("s3_constrained", "S3-constrained"), ("s3_full", "S3-full"),
               ("s4", "S4"), ("s5_metering", "S5-metering"), ("s5_oneway", "S5-bypass (unconditional)"),
               ("s5_oneway_yield", "S5-bypass (yielding)"), ("s2s4", "S2+S4 combined")]
```

### 5.1 Delay (time loss)

```{python}
#| label: tbl-timeloss-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Mean time loss (s/vehicle) by lambda — 7 main control variants, 10 seeds each"
frames = []
for prefix, label in SCEN_LABELS:
    d = pd.read_csv(f"../outputs/tables/{prefix}_lambda_summary.csv")
    d = d[d["metric"] == "mean_timeloss_s"][["lambda", "mean"]].copy()
    d["Scenario"] = label
    frames.append(d)
dfc = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
dfc = dfc.pivot(index="lambda", columns="Scenario", values="mean").round(1)
Markdown(dfc.to_markdown())
```

![Cross-scenario comparison by lambda — time loss (left) and collision count (right), mean +/- 95% CI](../outputs/figures/scenario_comparison_lambda.png){#fig-scenario-comparison width=95%}

**S1 (both modes)** has higher delay than S0 at **all five lambda
levels** — from about 40% at low demand to over 100% (fixed-time variant)
at high demand. **S4** sits essentially on top of S0 across the whole
lambda range. **S2** (with a real U-turn) is slightly above S0 at low/mid
lambda but essentially converges with it at lambda=1.4. **S3 (both
options)** shows a different pattern: a noticeable gap versus S0 at low
lambda (13-18% higher), which gradually shrinks as demand rises — the
classic roundabout pattern (a fixed geometric cost that dominates at low
demand, but becomes relatively less costly than the competing options as
demand rises).

### 5.2 Safety (recorded collisions and queuing)

```{python}
#| label: tbl-collision-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Mean recorded collision count per run, by lambda"
frames = []
for prefix, label in SCEN_LABELS:
    d = pd.read_csv(f"../outputs/tables/{prefix}_lambda_summary.csv")
    d = d[d["metric"] == "n_collisions"][["lambda", "mean"]].copy()
    d["Scenario"] = label
    frames.append(d)
dfc = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
dfc = dfc.pivot(index="lambda", columns="Scenario", values="mean").round(1)
Markdown(dfc.to_markdown())
```

Recorded collisions in S1 (both modes) are dramatically higher than S0 — at
lambda=1.4, the fixed-time variant records about 12x S0's collisions (root
cause analyzed in Section 6: mostly a product of queuing interacting with
uncalibrated aggressive behavior, not the signal itself). **S4** sits
essentially at S0's level across the whole lambda range. **S2** shows fewer
collisions than S0 at high lambda (not statistically significant, but
directional). **S3 (both options)** shows more collisions than S0,
especially the `full` variant at lambda=1.4 — likely partly an artifact of
this version's simple ring geometry (single lane, no engineered
deflection/island), not necessarily an inherent property of the roundabout
concept (see Sections 7 and 11).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-queue-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Observed maximum queue length (m), by lambda"
frames = []
for prefix, label in SCEN_LABELS:
    d = pd.read_csv(f"../outputs/tables/{prefix}_lambda_summary.csv")
    d = d[d["metric"] == "max_queue_length_m"][["lambda", "mean"]].copy()
    d["Scenario"] = label
    frames.append(d)
dfc = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
dfc = dfc.pivot(index="lambda", columns="Scenario", values="mean").round(1)
Markdown(dfc.to_markdown())
```

### 5.3 Statistical significance and effect size

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stats-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Paired comparison of each scenario against S0 on shared seeds — time loss"
dfstat = pd.read_csv("../outputs/tables/scenario_comparison.csv")
scen_map = {"s1_fixed": "S1-fixed", "s1_actuated": "S1-actuated",
            "s2": "S2", "s3_constrained": "S3-constrained", "s3_full": "S3-full", "s4": "S4",
            "s5_metering": "S5-metering", "s5_oneway": "S5-bypass (unconditional)",
            "s5_oneway_yield": "S5-bypass (yielding)", "s2s4": "S2+S4 combined"}
key = dfstat[(dfstat["metric"] == "mean_timeloss_s") &
             (dfstat["scenario"].isin(scen_map.keys()))][
    ["scenario", "lambda", "pct_diff", "p_value", "cohens_dz"]
].copy()
key.columns = ["Scenario", "lambda", "% diff vs. S0", "p-value (paired t)", "Cohen's dz"]
key["Scenario"] = key["Scenario"].map(scen_map)
Markdown(key.round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stats-collision
#| tbl-cap: "Paired comparison of S2/S3/S4/S5 against S0 — collision count and max queue length"
collision_scens = ["s2", "s3_constrained", "s3_full", "s4", "s5_metering", "s5_oneway", "s5_oneway_yield", "s2s4"]
key2 = dfstat[(dfstat["metric"].isin(["n_collisions", "max_queue_length_m"])) &
              (dfstat["scenario"].isin(collision_scens))][
    ["scenario", "lambda", "metric", "pct_diff", "p_value"]
].copy()
metric_en = {"n_collisions": "Collision count", "max_queue_length_m": "Max queue length"}
key2["metric"] = key2["metric"].map(metric_en)
key2["scenario"] = key2["scenario"].map(scen_map)
key2.columns = ["Scenario", "lambda", "Metric", "% diff vs. S0", "p-value"]
Markdown(key2.round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Significance summary: **S1 (both modes)** is significant and worse than S0
in all 10 delay comparisons, with large to very large effect sizes. **S4**
shows **no** significant delay difference from S0 at any lambda. **S2** is
significant (and slightly worse) only at lambda=0.6, 1.0 and 1.2; at
lambda=0.8 and 1.4 (peak demand) the difference is not significant. **S3
(both options, final revised geometry)** is significant and worse at most
low/mid lambda levels, but no longer significant at lambda=1.4 — the "fixed
geometric cost that fades as demand rises" pattern. **S5-metering** is
significant and worse at most lambda levels but not at lambda=1.4 (the
policy-relevant point). **S5-bypass, under both priority designs tested**,
is significant and worse than S0 at most lambda levels; the yielding
design is significant at all 5 lambda levels (see Section 7, mechanism 5,
for the full analysis of both designs).

**Standout result of this section: S2+S4 combined.** Unlike every scenario
above, this one shows a **strong, positive** safety result: collision
counts at lambda=1.0, 1.2 and 1.4 are 84%, 80% and 83% **lower** than S0
respectively — all three significant (p=0.046, 0.016, 0.001) with large to
very large effect sizes (Cohen's dz down to -1.58); max queue length is
also 60% and 71% lower at lambda=1.2 and 1.4 (significant). Delay is only
slightly worse (6-6%, significant) at lambda=0.6 and 1.0; at lambda=0.8,
1.2 and 1.4 the difference is not significant — and at lambda=1.4 it is
even directionally **better** than S0 (3.3% lower). That is, at high
demand (where it matters most), this scenario achieves dramatically better
safety **with no measurable delay cost** — the best delay+safety
combination in this study so far. See Section 7 for the mechanistic
interpretation and Section 9 for its place in the ranking.

On safety metrics for the remaining scenarios, none of S2/S3/S4/S5 show a
statistically significant difference from S0 at most lambda levels (high
variance in the 10-seed collision-count sample) — though the direction of
the differences (S2 better, S3/S5-bypass worse at high lambda) is notable.

## 6. Behavioral Sensitivity Diagnostic

Section 5's finding ("S1 worse than S0") is unexpected and could have two
roots: (a) the signal design itself (a fixed cycle on under-saturated
demand, Y ~ 0.59), or (b) interaction with this study's uncalibrated
aggressive behavioral parameters (short `tau`, `jmIgnoreFoeProb` up to 0.35
for motorcycles). To separate these, S0 and S1-fixed were rerun with
**SUMO's real default behavioral parameters** (not this study's aggressive
tuning; see `config/vtypes_diagnostic_default.yml`) on the same 5-lambda x
10-seed grid (`src/09_behavior_diagnostic.py`, 100 independent runs,
separate from the formal scenario registry).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-diagnostic
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic: time loss with SUMO default (non-aggressive) behavior"
diag = pd.read_csv("../outputs/tables/diag_behavior_default_comparison.csv")
diag.columns = ["lambda", "Mean S1-fixed (default behavior)", "Mean S0 (default behavior)",
                 "% diff", "p-value"]
Markdown(diag.round(2).to_markdown(index=False))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-diagnostic-collision
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic: mean collision count with SUMO default behavior"
dlam = pd.read_csv("../outputs/tables/diag_behavior_default_lambda_summary.csv")
dcol = dlam[dlam["metric"] == "n_collisions"][["scenario", "lambda", "mean"]].copy()
dcol["scenario"] = dcol["scenario"].map({"diag_s0": "S0 (default behavior)",
                                           "diag_s1_fixed": "S1-fixed (default behavior)"})
dcol = dcol.pivot(index="lambda", columns="scenario", values="mean")
Markdown(dcol.to_markdown())
```

**Two distinct, complementary results:**

1. **Delay:** even with default (non-aggressive) behavior, S1-fixed is
   still 36-57% more delayed than S0 (all 5 comparisons significant). That
   is, **most of the delay effect really does come from the signal design
   itself** — imposing a stop behind red on demand that, absent a signal,
   could merge without a full stop; aggressive behavior amplifies this
   effect (40-105% in the main study) but does not create it.
2. **Safety:** with default behavior, collision counts for **both**
   scenarios are near zero (at most 0.4 per run, versus hundreds under the
   aggressive parameters). That is, **the collision explosion seen in
   Section 5.2 is almost entirely a product of signal-induced queuing
   interacting with uncalibrated aggressive behavioral parameters — not an
   inherent property of the signal itself.**

This decomposition sharpens Phase 4's message: S1's delay problem is a real
engineering finding (signal design on under-saturated demand); S1's safety
problem is mostly a **warning about behavioral calibration**, not a verdict
on signals being inherently dangerous.

## 7. Discussion and Interpretation

With the Section 6 diagnostic factored in, three candidate explanations for
Section 5's finding can now be weighted:

**1. Design demand was under-saturated (Y ~ 0.59) — the dominant delay
mechanism, confirmed.** When traffic volume is clearly under capacity, a
fixed-cycle signal forces vehicles that could otherwise merge immediately
without a full stop (zipper/priority) to stop behind red. Section 6's
diagnostic showed this mechanism **alone** (with no aggressive behavior at
all) is enough to make S1 36-57% slower than S0.

**2. Interaction with the uncalibrated aggressive behavioral model — the
dominant safety mechanism, confirmed.** Examining collision locations
(Section 5.2) showed the overwhelming majority of S1's collisions occur **in
the queue behind the signal**, not at the junction point itself. Section
6's diagnostic settled this: with default behavior, collisions nearly
disappear. **It is not that the signal is inherently unsafe; it is
signal-induced queuing meeting modeled aggressive driving culture (short
follower time gap, motorcycle disregard for right-of-way) that produces
collisions.**

**3. Node-type conversion from zipper to traffic_light — a small,
secondary contribution.** Examining collision locations showed the share of
collisions *inside* signalized junctions (not on the approach links) is
small (under 5% of the total) — this mechanism may contribute a small
share, but the dominant mechanism is #2 above (queuing).

**A complementary result from S2/S4:** S4 (which adds no active control,
only channelizes the right-turn conflict) shows no significant difference
from S0; S2 (which fully removes the left-turn conflict, also with no
active control) is essentially tied with S0 at peak demand and shows
better collision/queue numbers. This pattern — "removing a geometric
conflict without adding active control performs at least as well as (and
sometimes better than) adding uncalibrated active control" — is exactly
what mechanisms 1 and 2 above predict.

**4. Why is S3 (roundabout) worse than S0 at low demand, but improves as
demand rises?** This pattern (Sections 5.1/5.3) is fully consistent with
roundabout engineering literature: a roundabout, even a small one, imposes
a **fixed geometric cost** on every vehicle (slowing to enter/deflect,
longer circulating path versus a straight line) that, at low demand — when
there is effectively no competing cost from the alternative (a straight
zipper merge) — looks like pure overhead versus the existing condition; but
as demand rises, the existing condition (S0) degrades faster (because the
implicit coordination of zipper merging breaks down under congestion),
while the roundabout — as long as it has spare capacity — degrades more
slowly; the result is the gradual convergence of the two curves seen in the
data. **S3's elevated collision count** (especially the `full` variant at
high lambda) is likely largely an artifact of this conceptual
implementation's simplicity: the ring was built with single lanes and no
engineered deflection/island (see `scenarios/S3_roundabout/README.md`) — a
real roundabout with an engineered radius/deflection would likely
substantially reduce this side effect; this finding should be read as
"needs more careful geometric design before a final judgment," not "the
roundabout concept is inherently unsafe."

**5. Why do S5's two variants, built on the same S3-constrained ring,
produce such different results?** Both S5 options start from the same
baseline (the unmodified S3-constrained ring); the difference in outcome
comes directly from the type of intervention added:

- **Metering** adds no *further* control point — it places a single-node
  signal on the main receiver of deck traffic to regulate entry into the
  ring. Comparison with the bare S3-constrained ring shows this signal
  **genuinely works**: at lambda=1.4, max queue length drops from 147 m
  (bare ring) to 106 m, and delay/collisions are also slightly better —
  i.e., metering absorbs part of the small roundabout's queue-overflow risk
  at high demand, exactly the role a metering signal is supposed to play.
  It still does not reach S0's level, however.
- **The north-south bypass**, in its first cut, added a **new, unresolved
  geometric conflict point** — exactly what netconvert flagged with an
  "intersecting left turns" warning at build time: "Intersecting left turns
  at junction 6711509176 from lane s5_bypass_N_S_0 and lane
  610531293#0-AddedOffRampEdge_1 (increase junction radius to avoid
  this)." In that version, at lambda=1.4, delay reached 56.3 s (+106% vs.
  S0) and about 1,199 collisions per run (roughly 12x S0's) — numbers that
  land almost exactly on **S1-fixed's own worst case** (56.0 s, 1,256
  collisions/run), despite a completely different mechanism (a geometry
  defect, not a traffic light).

**The geometric fix, and its honest result (this session):** exactly as
netconvert itself suggested, `radius="10"` was set on the conflicting
junction node and the full network/simulation batch was rebuilt and rerun
(see `scenarios/S5_hybrid/README.md` for the full account). **The warning
was completely eliminated — but the simulated result showed no reliable
improvement.** At lambda=1.4, mean delay actually rose to 61.7 s (+126%) —
a larger number than before, not smaller — though it is no longer
statistically significant (p=0.130, versus a significant result in the
previous version) because between-seed variance rose sharply. The reason
is clear from the per-seed breakdown: **9 of the 10 seeds** now cluster
around a more reasonable mean than before (~42 s delay, ~660 collisions —
better than the pre-fix version), but **one seed (seed 10) collapses
completely**: 242 s of delay and **6,009 collisions in a single run**. For
comparison, S5-metering's worst seed at the same lambda is only 44 s / 483
collisions — the geometric fix did not remove the bypass's sensitivity to
seed (its tail risk).

**This is an honest negative result, not an unreported failure:** the fix
was applied exactly per netconvert's own diagnostic and fully resolved its
documented warning; this shows **that specific warning was a symptom of a
real but secondary geometric issue, not the primary driver of the bypass's
poor performance.** The initial hypothesis was that the primary driver was
mechanism 2 above: granting unconditional priority (edge priority 80,
`pass="true"`, higher than the ring) to a fast through-movement across an
already-congested junction, once it interacts with this study's
uncalibrated aggressive behavioral parameters, is prone to a bistable
collapse pattern — most seeds settle into a bad but stable state, and
occasionally (here, 1 in 10) the system cascades into a fully uncontrolled
collision chain.

**A direct test of the hypothesis (Section 12, this session continued):**
if the root cause really is "unconditional priority," removing it should
help. To test this, `oneway_yield` was built: the identical bypass
topology, but the edge priority was lowered from 80 to **30** (below the
ring's 50) and `pass="true"` was removed — the bypass now has to find a
gap like any other normal priority-junction connection in this network
(exactly like S0/S4). **The result was the opposite of the hypothesis:**
instead of improving, collision count at lambda=1.4 rose to 1,526.5 per
run (higher than either prior design) — and this time it was not a rare
tail collapse but a **uniformly bad outcome across all 10 seeds** (ranging
428-4,498 collisions), now cleanly statistically significant (p=0.017
delay, p=0.010 collisions, at every lambda level). Removing unconditional
priority turned a rare, catastrophic collapse into a chronic, predictable
weakness — not better, just **differently** bad. A plausible mechanism: forcing
the bypass to negotiate right-of-way on every pass (instead of guaranteed
through movement) itself creates a new sudden stop/slowdown point that, with
this study's short follower time gap and aggressive right-of-way disregard,
turns into collisions — essentially S1's own queuing mechanism (mechanism
2), recurring at a different location. **A stronger conclusion than
before:** neither unconditional priority nor normal yielding priority makes
this bypass acceptable; the mere existence of this added conflict point,
regardless of its priority design, is the problem. **This tail risk /
chronic weakness finding is itself a separate and important safety
result** — and a concrete illustration of the exact statistical limitation
Section 11 already flags about collision-count confidence intervals with a
10-seed sample. A real fix likely requires an actual traffic signal on the
bypass (like S1, with the same behavioral-calibration caveats) or full
grade separation — not any further priority/right-of-way adjustment — see
Section 12.

**Summary for S5:** metering — which adds complementary control to an
existing geometric conflict — performs better than the raw ring and is
also more robust (lower tail risk). The bypass — which adds a new
geometric conflict with no active control — retained a bad mean and a
safety problem (as either tail risk or chronic weakness) under **both**
priority designs tested, even after its specific geometric warning was
documented, targeted, and successfully resolved. This pattern is fully
consistent with mechanisms 1 and 2 above and confirms them at the level of
scenario design, not just S1's single-node design: **complementary control
on an existing conflict helps; a new conflict with no active control does
not help, regardless of its priority design or how "clean" its geometry
is.**

**6. Why does S2+S4 combined give this study's best safety result?** This
scenario directly tested the prediction of mechanisms 1 and 2 above at a
larger scale: instead of removing one type of conflict (left-turn or
right-turn), both are removed simultaneously — with no new active control
added. The result is an 80-84% reduction in collisions (significant, large
effect size) at lambda >= 1.0, without worsening delay at peak demand. This
is consistent with an "additive" hypothesis: because S2's nodes (diverges)
and S4's nodes (merges) are entirely separate, two independent conflict
reductions on two different node sets show a **cumulative**, not
competing or cancelling, effect — unlike, say, S5, where adding a new
conflict (the bypass) next to a good intervention (the roundabout)
neutralized or reversed the positive effect. **The broader lesson for
scenario design:** when independent interventions, with no active control,
act on non-overlapping physical junctions, cumulative benefit can be
expected; when an intervention itself adds a new conflict (rather than
only removing an existing one), that cumulative benefit is not guaranteed
and can reverse.

**What this means for the report:** the "S1 worse than S0" finding should
not be read as a definitive verdict on the real-world value of traffic
signals. It says: **a simple Webster-designed signal on under-saturated
demand, without complementary coordination/channelization and without
behavioral calibration, can backfire** — that is itself a valuable
engineering finding, not a model weakness. Likewise, S3's finding says "a
simple conceptual roundabout is not a winner at low demand," not "the
roundabout concept is rejected"; and S5's finding says "adding
complementary control to an imperfect geometric intervention can offset
part of its weakness, but adding a new, uncontrolled geometric conflict
point breaks it" — not that "combining a roundabout with smart control is
inherently useless." And S2+S4's finding says "combining independent
interventions with no active control, on non-overlapping junctions, can
give a cumulative benefit" — the strongest evidence in this study yet for
a "remove the geometric conflict first, save active control for after
calibration" approach.

## 8. Scenario SWOT Analysis

For all 6 main scenarios (S0 through S5) and the S2+S4 combined scenario,
the points below are grounded in **real simulated data** (uncalibrated) —
no scenario remains purely conceptual/without data.

| Scenario | Strengths | Weaknesses | Opportunities | Threats |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S0 — existing condition** | Lowest/tied-lowest delay in current data; zero implementation cost; zipper merging behaves smoothly at moderate demand | No formal control, dependent on driver skill/caution; collision count grows exponentially with lambda (Phase 3: up to 80x from lambda=0.6 to 1.4); no clear right-of-way for left turns | Zero cost to keep as baseline; improvable via S4 (light channelization, no active-control cost) | As Kerman's demand grows, the collision rate could quickly become unacceptable |
| **S1 — signal (fixed/actuated)** | Formal, predictable right-of-way; actuated self-adapts to demand fluctuation; infrastructure ready for future coordination | **Data-driven, not hypothetical:** more delayed than S0 even with default behavior (Section 6); more collisions (but this is mostly a product of uncalibrated aggressive behavior, not the signal itself) | Behavioral calibration and/or signal coordination could reverse the result; actuated is clearly better than fixed-time | Early implementation without behavioral calibration could make the safety situation practically worse |
| **S2 — left-turn removal + real U-turn** | Not significantly different from S0 in delay at lambda=0.8 and 1.4 (peak demand); directionally better collisions/queue at high lambda; no active control (no S1-style queuing risk); negligible sensitivity to U-turn distance (150/250/350 m) | Slightly (7-12%) higher delay than S0 at lambda=0.6, 1.0 and 1.2 — the real cost of the U-turn detour, unlike the optimistic first cut, is now in the model and tempers the benefit | A more precise geometric version (real curvature, adequate acceleration length) could reduce the fixed cost | Real left-turn count data (not the 15% assumption) could shift this finding in either direction |
| **S3 — asymmetric roundabout (constrained/full)** | Gap versus S0 shrinks and becomes non-significant as demand rises (the conventional roundabout pattern); the `full` variant (open center bay) is slightly better than `constrained` at mid/high delay | Significantly worse than S0 at low/mid demand (lambda <= 1.0); more collisions in both variants (directional, likely largely an artifact of this version's simple single-lane, non-engineered ring geometry); the `full` option is conditional on a structural sign-off outside this study's scope | Precise geometric design (real radius/deflection/island) could meaningfully improve the result; if structurally approved, the center bay gives a real benefit | Without better geometric design, this version's safety risk could recur in the real world; delay in structural approval keeps the `full` option effectively unimplementable |
| **S4 — channelization** | Lowest-cost/lowest-risk intervention; no new junction node or structural sign-off needed; no statistically significant difference from S0 on any metric (neither better nor worse, at all 5 lambda levels) | No measurable improvement in this implementation; alone, does not remove the informal left turn | Could be a fast/low-risk intermediate step, or combine with S2 (which removes the left-turn conflict) for a cumulative effect — see next steps | May only mask symptoms rather than the root cause (no formal right-of-way for left turns) |
| **S5 — hybrid (metering/bypass)** | Metering genuinely improves on the bare S3-constrained ring at lambda=1.4 (max queue 106 m vs. 147 m) and is more robust (worst single seed only 44 s / 483 collisions); its 20 s cycle was empirically checked, not just assumed; all three built variants share the ring infrastructure from S3 | The bypass failed under **both** priority designs tested: unconditional (priority 80) still had a severe tail risk even after its documented geometric conflict was fully resolved (1 of 10 seeds collapsed completely, 6,009 collisions in one run); yielding (priority 30, built specifically to fix that risk) turned it into a uniform, statistically significant weakness across all 10 seeds instead (lambda=1.4: 1,526.5 collisions/run) — worse, not better; neither variant yet reaches S0's level | Metering could move closer to S0 with behavioral calibration; for the bypass, two rejected fixes show the real next step is active control with an actual signal (not another priority adjustment) or grade separation | Without active control, the bypass could reproduce in the real world either a rare-but-catastrophic collapse (unconditional priority) or chronic congestion (yielding priority) — no simple priority scheme makes this location safe |
| **S2+S4 combined** | **This study's best safety result:** 80-84% fewer collisions than S0 at lambda >= 1.0 (all significant, large effect sizes); max queue length down to 71% lower at lambda=1.4; even delay at lambda=1.4 is directionally better than S0 (not worse); needed no new code — just calling two existing S2/S4 functions on one network; no active control, no S1-style queuing risk | Delay slightly (6-6%) worse, significant, at lambda=0.6 and 1.0; inherits every explicit limitation of S2 (assumed U-turn share) and S4 (no curbside-parking model effect); the "additive" hypothesis was confirmed by data for this specific pair, but was not guaranteed in advance | A natural, immediate candidate for the next implementation step — low cost, no structural sign-off, no active control; the "combine independent interventions on non-overlapping junctions" pattern may generalize to other scenario pairs | Conditional on real behavioral calibration (Section 10) before any firm implementation recommendation; real left/right-turn count data could shift the size of this benefit |

## 9. Preliminary Conclusions and Ranking

::: {.callout-warning}
## This is not a final ranking
All 6 main scenarios plus the S2+S4 combined scenario have now been built,
simulated, and given a qualitative/SWOT analysis (Sections 7 and 8). The
ranking below is **based solely on available data** and, absent real
calibration (Section 10), should not be the basis for an implementation
decision; S3 and S5 each need a more serious round of geometric/control
revision before a final judgment (Section 12).
:::

Based on current evidence, a preliminary ranking (best to worst, based on a
combination of delay + safety across the lambda range, with particular
weight on behavior at peak demand lambda=1.4):

1. **S2+S4 combined — this study's best safety result, at the top of the
   ranking.** An 80-84% reduction in collisions versus S0 at lambda >= 1.0
   (all significant, large effect sizes), max queue length down to 71%
   lower, and delay at lambda=1.4 directionally **better** than S0 (not
   worse) — with no active control or new code (just combining two
   existing fixes, S2 and S4). The only cost: slightly (6-6%) worse delay
   at lambda=0.6 and 1.0. This combination was built directly from this
   study's own recurring observation ("removing a geometric conflict
   without active control performs at least as well, and sometimes
   better") and confirmed that observation with the strongest evidence yet.
2. **S0 (existing condition) and S4 (channelization, alone) — effectively
   tied, second tier.** S4 showed no statistically significant difference
   from S0 on any metric; i.e., this lowest-risk single intervention is at
   minimum harmless and has a low implementation cost.
3. **S2 (left-turn removal + real U-turn, alone) — close behind, with a
   real edge at peak demand.** Accounting for the real cost of the U-turn
   detour (not modeled in this report's first cut), S2 is slightly (7-12%)
   worse than S0 at low/mid demand, but at exactly lambda=1.4 — the demand
   level of most concern for this intersection's future — it remains **not
   significantly different** from S0 and is directionally safer.
   Sensitivity to U-turn distance (150/250/350 m) was negligible.
4. **S3 (asymmetric roundabout, both options) and S5-metering — need more
   careful geometric/control design before a final judgment, but with
   promising evidence.** S3 is significantly worse than S0 at low/mid
   demand (both delay and directionally in collisions), but the gap shrinks
   quickly as demand rises — the conventional roundabout pattern.
   **S5-metering** goes one step further: compared to the bare
   S3-constrained ring, it is genuinely **better** at lambda=1.4 (max queue
   106 m vs. 147 m, and more robust — worst single seed only 44 s / 483
   collisions) — direct evidence that even an untuned metering signal can
   offset part of a small roundabout's inherent weakness at peak demand.
   Both of these conceptual implementations (a single-lane ring with no
   engineered deflection) most likely represent something close to the
   worst case for these concepts; no definitive judgment about the real
   value of "a roundabout" or "a roundabout + metering" can be drawn from
   this data.
5. **S1 (signal, both modes) and S5-bypass (both priority designs), as
   currently implemented — not recommended.** Section 6's diagnostic showed
   S1 would remain worse than S0 even under hypothetically calibrated
   behavior (the primary delay mechanism is the signal design, not
   behavior); the actuated variant is clearly preferable to fixed-time.
   **S5-bypass** was tested twice and failed both times: with unconditional
   priority, even after its documented geometric conflict was fully and
   successfully resolved (the netconvert warning is gone), it showed a
   severe tail risk — 9 of 10 seeds cluster around ~42 s, but one seed
   collapses completely (242 s, 6,009 collisions in a single run), a scale
   that exceeds even **S1-fixed's own worst case** (56.0 s, 1,256
   collisions/run). With normal yielding priority (lower than the ring, no
   unconditional right-of-way — a direct test of the hypothesis that
   removing unconditional priority would help), the result reversed:
   collisions at lambda=1.4 rose to 1,526.5 per run, this time uniformly
   across all 10 seeds rather than a rare collapse, and cleanly
   statistically significant. This shows neither a purely geometric fix nor
   a priority-design change is enough for this scenario; the root cause is
   the same behavioral mechanism shared with S1 — see Section 7 (mechanism
   5) for the full analysis.

**Process recommendation:** **S2+S4 combined** is now the strongest
candidate for the next implementation step — low cost, no active control,
and this study's best safety evidence; S4 alone (low-risk, no negative
effect) and S2 alone (promising at peak demand) are its natural backups.
All of these recommendations are **conditional on real behavioral
calibration** (since Section 6 showed the safety result is highly
sensitive to these parameters). S3 and S5-metering need a more serious
round of geometric/control design (not just this version's conceptual ring
or netconvert's default cycle) before a fair comparison; S5-bypass now
needs genuine active control (not a priority/geometry adjustment) to move
out of S1's tier.

## 10. Calibration and Validation Plan

Part of this report's value is being explicit about the data we do not have.
Section 6's diagnostic confirmed this prioritization: **behavioral
calibration (third row of the table) is now a critical priority, tied with
turning-movement counts.**

| Data need | Suggested collection method | Cost/time | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15-minute turning-movement counts, AM and PM peaks | Drone/elevated-camera video + automated counting (YOLO + ByteTrack) | Moderate | **Critical** |
| Fleet composition and motorcycle share | Same video | Low | High |
| Queue length and clearance time | Same video | Low | High |
| **Behavioral parameters (tau, jmIgnoreFoeProb, real follower gap in queue)** | Vehicle trajectory extraction from video + Optuna/GA fitting | Moderate | **Critical (confirmed by the Phase-4 diagnostic)** |
| Saturation flow | Standard field measurement | Low | Medium |
| Route travel time | GPS floating car, 6-10 runs per peak | Low | High |
| Regional OD | Ride-hailing / mobile data / interviews | High | Version 2 |

**Acceptance criteria:** GEH < 5 for >= 85% of movements, travel-time error
< 15%, and qualitative agreement in the queuing pattern. Validation is
performed on a held-out period (e.g., a different day's peak).

## 11. Limitations

- **This report is an uncalibrated model** (see the banner at the top of
  the report) — no absolute number (seconds, collision count) should be
  read as a real-world prediction; only the relative direction and
  magnitude of differences is valid.
- **All 6 main scenarios plus the S2+S4 combined scenario have been built,
  simulated, and given a qualitative/SWOT analysis** (Sections 7 and 8),
  but Section 9's conclusion remains preliminary and conditional on real
  calibration — and neither S3 nor S5-metering (both built on the same
  conceptual S3 ring) has been tested with finalized geometry/control.
- **S2+S4 combined**, despite giving this study's best safety result,
  inherits two assumptions it did not itself introduce: S2's assumed 15%
  U-turn share and S4's not modeling the curbside-parking effect. The
  "additive" hypothesis was confirmed by data only for this specific pair;
  generalizing to other combinations (e.g. S2+S1) is not guaranteed in
  advance.
- **S3 (both options) is a deliberately simplified geometric
  implementation, though improved:** the ring's shape is now an arc (not
  the first cut's straight line) drawn between 4 real points, but it is
  still not an engineered roundabout with a designed radius/deflection/
  splitter island. A single-lane-vs.-two-lane experiment (see
  `scenarios/S3_roundabout/README.md`) showed adding a lane *increases*
  collisions rather than reducing them — a finding future, more precise
  geometric design should take into account.
- **S5 remains a first-cut/exploratory scenario, though revised twice:**
  the `metering` signal's 20 s cycle was confirmed with a light empirical
  sweep (3 seeds, not a formal optimization method). The bypass was tested
  under two priority designs, both rejected: `oneway_priority`'s documented
  geometric conflict (a netconvert "intersecting left turns" warning) was
  fully resolved, but that fix produced no reliable improvement — mean
  delay at peak demand got worse, and a serious tail risk (1 seed in 10
  collapsing completely) remained. `oneway_yield`, built specifically to
  test whether removing that unconditional priority would help, instead
  made things worse — the rare collapse became a uniform, statistically
  significant weakness across all 10 seeds. This shows the bypass's problem
  is not the geometry (now fixed) or the specific priority scheme (both
  ends of the spectrum tested), but the mere presence of this added
  conflict point interacting with the study's aggressive behavior
  parameters; an actual traffic signal or full grade separation have not
  yet been tested.
- **S2 now accounts for the real cost of the U-turn detour** (fixing the
  previous version of this report's limitation), but it is still an
  approximation: the share of traffic routed to the U-turn (15%) comes from
  `turn_ratio_baseline.left`, not a real count; and the U-turn's
  entry/exit geometry is not a fully engineered design.
- **S1's signal design is an explicit simplification:** rather than one
  classical intersection, independent merge nodes were signalized (see
  Section 4). Coordination (progression/offset) between these nodes was
  not modeled — it could offset part of the observed negative effect.
- Ramp turning radii, bridge bay widths, and baseline demand still come
  from visual estimation / engineering judgment, not field measurement
  (see the full assumptions table in `config/assumptions.yml`).
- The collision-count confidence interval is computed with the standard
  t-based method (suited to continuous data); a Poisson/negative-binomial
  model would be more appropriate for rare-event counts. This matters
  especially for S3 and S5-bypass, where collision variance is high
  (several directionally strong comparisons were not statistically
  significant with a 10-seed sample; S5-bypass at lambda=1.4 is a concrete
  example — a single seed out of 10 alone pulls the mean from about 42 s to
  61.7 s).
- This English report was synchronized with the Persian version in this
  session; because both reports read from the same
  `outputs/tables/*.csv` files, the numbers in the two languages always
  stay identical, but later edits to the Persian text still need to be
  carried over to English by hand — as this session did immediately after
  making those edits.

## 12. Next Steps (Phase 4, continued)

1. **An actual traffic signal or grade separation for the S5 bypass** — two
   prior attempts, both this session, have been ruled out: a purely
   geometric fix (the junction radius) resolved netconvert's warning but
   produced no real improvement; lowering the bypass to normal yielding
   priority (`oneway_yield`) did not help either — it turned the rare tail
   collapse into a uniform, statistically significant weakness (Section 7,
   mechanism 5). The reasonable range of priority/geometry adjustments for
   this location has now been tried and rejected; the real next step is not
   another priority tweak but an actual signal on the bypass itself (like
   S1, with its cycle timed, and the same behavioral-calibration caveats)
   or full grade separation — still the top priority on this list.
2. **Limited behavioral calibration** (Section 10) — now the top priority
   after item 1, because **S2+S4 combined** (item 3 in the previous version
   of this list, now built and simulated — see Sections 5, 7, 8, 9) is the
   current best implementation candidate, and its safety result, like every
   other scenario in this study, is sensitive to uncalibrated behavioral
   parameters; also needed before any implementation recommendation
   regarding S1 or S5-bypass.
3. **More precise S3 geometric design:** replace the current single-lane
   arc ring with a real roundabout (engineered radius/deflection/splitter
   island) — S3's current result is still likely more pessimistic than a
   real engineered design; this automatically carries over to S5-metering,
   since it is built on the same ring.
4. Global sensitivity analysis (Sobol/factorial) over lambda, left-turn
   share, motorcycle share, tau, and turning radius — now including S2+S4,
   to see how robust its safety benefit is to peak demand and turn-share
   assumptions.
5. Replace the t-based confidence interval for collision counts with a
   rare-event model (Poisson/negative binomial) — S5-bypass just gave a
   fresh, concrete illustration of why this is needed (Section 11).
6. Investigate further combinations (e.g. **S2+S4+metering**) now that
   independent interventions on non-overlapping junctions have been shown
   to give a cumulative effect (Section 7, mechanism 6).
